extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters of New York; delegates and policymakers considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution; readers interested in constitutional design and federal powers
extracted.subtask_description: A persuasive political-constitutional essay arguing standards for an effective national government and criticizing defects of the Articles of Confederation; intended to guide ratification debates and design of federal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government should raise its own revenues (avoid quotas/requisitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorize the national government to raise its own revenues rather than rely on requisitions or quotas imposed on the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotas and requisitions produce glaring inequality and extreme oppression because ability to pay varies widely; allowing the Union to levy imposts and excises lets contributions 'in a degree be at [a citizen's] own option' and avoids the injustices and enforcement difficulties of apportioning contributions among States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect taxes (imposts/excises) as chief revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposts, excises, and duties on consumption should constitute the chief part of federal revenue since they self-limit and are less likely to produce private oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect taxes 'prescribe their own limit' — if duties are too high they lessen consumption and revenue, which acts as a natural check against excess; inequalities across States from particular duties will likely be counterbalanced by duties on other objects over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: If direct taxes used, apportion by population rather than land valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct taxes (principally on land and buildings) may admit of a rule of apportionment; population counts are preferred over land valuation for simplicity and certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtaining accurate land valuation is 'a herculean task' and especially impracticable in an imperfectly settled country; the expense and difficulty of valuation make numbers (population) a more feasible standard for apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: No common measure of national wealth — avoid a single fixed rule for State contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because wealth depends on many complex and variable causes, there can be 'no common measure of national wealth' and therefore no general or stationary rule to determine a State's ability to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to fix contributions by a single rule will produce inequality and oppression; this supports vesting revenue-raising authority in the national government rather than rigid apportionment schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal power to regulate commerce (domestic and foreign)
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must have the power to regulate commerce with other nations and between the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of federal regulation has hindered treaties and created interstate dissatisfaction; separate and conflicting State regulations can frustrate uniform foreign relations and commercial policy (example: multiplicity of duties in the German empire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent obstructive and conflicting State commercial regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: State prohibitions, restrictions, and exclusions that conflict with national interests must be restrained by general authority to avoid animosity and impediments to interstate intercourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without concerted national control, the 'interfering and unneighborly regulations' of individual States will multiply, treating citizens of other States as aliens and undermining the Union's commercial advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority to raise and maintain armies and fleets directly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union should be empowered to levy troops, build and equip fleets, and provide for their government and support directly, rather than by requisitioning quotas from States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requisitions during the late war led to competition among States, inflated bounties, short enlistments, and fluctuations destructive to discipline; direct federal authority avoids these inefficiencies and inequities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotas and requisitions (for men or money) are impracticable and unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems of quotas and requisitions are 'a system of imbecility' that create inequality, injustice, and operational failure whether applied to soldiers or money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such systems produce bidding wars, inadequate levies in emergencies, and inability to account for deficiencies in manpower; they also fail as a reliable means of national defense or finance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should be proportionate to population; equal suffrage among States is objectionable
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of equal suffrage among unequal States (one State, one vote) contradicts principles of proportion and fair representation and can allow a small number of States to control national decisions contrary to the majority of people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal State votes may make a majority of States a minority of the people; large States would resent receiving laws from much smaller States, risking revolt and undermining republican principles where the sense of the majority should prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive supermajority or unanimity requirements that empower minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring more than a simple majority for important decisions gives minorities a de facto negative that can obstruct the majority and substitute partisan or corrupt influences for public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Congress functioning like a 'Polish diet' where nonattendance or a single vote can halt business; high thresholds facilitate foreign corruption, intrigue, and paralysis at critical moments such as war or treaty-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a supreme judiciary to ensure uniform interpretation of laws and treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and treaties are 'a dead letter' without courts to expound them; there must be one supreme tribunal under the authority that forms treaties to produce uniform final determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple State courts of final jurisdiction could produce contradictory decisions and allow local bias to trump national law; a single paramount court avoids confusion and secures the force of national engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties (and national laws) require uniform final adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Because treaties are part of the law of the land, their 'true import' must be ascertained by judicial determinations ultimately resolved by a national supreme tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such a tribunal, treaties and national laws would be subject to the prejudices and differing opinions of many legislatures and courts, undermining foreign confidence and national honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional authority must rest on the consent of the people, not merely State legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government's foundation ought to be 'THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE' rather than ratification solely by State legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratification by legislatures has exposed the federal system to questions of validity and to the notion that a party to a compact can repeal it; popular ratification grounds the Union in legitimate, original authority and prevents facile repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be proportioned to ends — powers coextensive with entrusted objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The persons charged with attaining an end must possess the means required to attain it; constitutional powers should be coextensive with the objects of federal administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because national exigencies are unpredictable and varied, no constitutional shackles should be imposed on powers essential to formation, direction, or support of national forces and interests; powers appropriate to national objects may safely accompany those objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate objects between federal and state authorities and vest commensurate powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which objects belong to federal versus local governments and give each the fullest authority necessary to fulfill their assigned purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Union should handle common defense, foreign commerce, and national intercourse; local governments should manage internal justice and other provincial matters; failing to provide powers commensurate with ends would violate prudence and imperil national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative organization must fit the scope of powers and avoid concentration of prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization of the legislative body (e.g., a single assembly) may be proper for limited, fettered authorities but is inconsistent with entrusting extensive sovereign powers to one body; unchecked accumulation risks tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the single assembly is later supplemented with additional powers, either the structure will fail from weakness or successive augmentations will accumulate prerogatives in a single body, producing an 'execrable form of government' contrary to republican principles.
